events.title: Early Iron Age Settlement
events.description: Archaeological evidence shows human settlement in present-day Guinea during the Iron Age. Early inhabitants mastered iron-working technology and developed agriculture and pastoralism. These early societies laid the foundation for later complex political structures.

events.title: Mande Migration
events.description: Mande-speaking groups migrated south from the upper Niger River region, settling in present-day Guinea. They brought advanced agricultural techniques, iron-working, and political organization. The Mande became the dominant ethnic group, establishing numerous small kingdoms and chiefdoms.

events.title: Ghana Empire Influence
events.description: While the Ghana Empire's core was further north, its trade networks and political influence extended into northern Guinea. Gold and salt trade routes crossed the region, promoting economic development and cultural exchange.

events.title: Mali Empire Establishment
events.description: After Sundiata Keita established the Mali Empire, most of present-day Guinea became part of the empire. Mali controlled important gold-producing regions and trade routes, with Guinea's Bure goldfields becoming a major source of imperial wealth.

events.title: Spread of Islam
events.description: Through trans-Saharan trade and Mali Empire influence, Islam began spreading in northern Guinea. Muslim merchants and scholars established Islamic learning centers, though traditional religious beliefs remained prevalent in many areas.

events.title: Songhai Empire Rule
events.description: After the Songhai Empire rose, it controlled northern Guinea regions. The empire continued developing trans-Saharan trade, with Guinea's gold mines providing important revenue. This period witnessed further fusion of Islamic culture with local traditions.

events.title: First Portuguese Arrival
events.description: Portuguese explorer Nuno Tristão first reached Guinea's coast. The Portuguese were attracted by the region's rich gold resources and began establishing trading posts. This marked the beginning of direct European contact with Guinea.

events.title: European Trading Posts
events.description: Portugal, later France, Britain and other European nations established trading posts along Guinea's coast. Main trade goods included gold, ivory, pepper and later slaves. These posts became outposts of European colonial expansion.

events.title: Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade
events.description: Guinea became an important source for the trans-Atlantic slave trade. Hundreds of thousands of Guineans were forcibly transported to American plantations. The slave trade severely disrupted local social structures, causing population decline and political instability.

events.title: Futa Jallon Islamic State
events.description: Fulani Muslims established the Futa Jallon Islamic state in Guinea's central highlands. This theocratic state controlled important trade routes and became a major Islamic learning center in West Africa. The state implemented strict Islamic law and traded with European coastal posts.

events.title: French Colonial Expansion Begins
events.description: France began establishing more permanent footholds on Guinea's coast. French officer Louis Faidherbe signed treaties with local chiefs, establishing French influence in the region. This marked the beginning of French colonial rule.

events.title: Samori Touré Resistance
events.description: Mandinka leader Samori Touré established the Wassoulou Empire, leading armed resistance against French colonial expansion. His army used modern weapons and conducted 17 years of guerrilla warfare. Samori's capture in 1898 marked the end of the last major resistance.

events.title: French Guinea Established
events.description: France formally established the French Guinea colony, appointing the first colonial governor. France implemented direct rule, establishing administrative systems and beginning large-scale exploitation of the region's natural resources.

events.title: Incorporation into French West Africa
events.description: French Guinea became part of the French West Africa federation, headquartered in Dakar. This administrative reorganization strengthened French control over West African colonies and promoted regional economic integration.

events.title: Forced Labor System
events.description: France implemented a forced labor system in Guinea, compelling locals to build railways, roads and other infrastructure. Thousands died under harsh working conditions. This system caused widespread resentment and resistance.

events.title: Conakry-Niger Railway Construction
events.description: France built a railway connecting Conakry port to the interior to facilitate bauxite mining and transport. Railway construction used extensive forced labor but also promoted economic development and modernization.

events.title: Bauxite Mining Begins
events.description: France began large-scale exploitation of Guinea's rich bauxite resources. Guinea possesses the world's largest bauxite reserves, and mining became the backbone of the colonial economy. However, profits mainly flowed to France with limited local benefits.

events.title: French Overseas Territory Status
events.description: Post-war, Guinea gained French overseas territory status with representation in the French parliament. This change gave Guineans more political rights and laid the foundation for later independence movements.

events.title: Democratic Party of Guinea Founded
events.description: Ahmed Sékou Touré founded the Democratic Party of Guinea (PDG), the country's first modern political party. The party advocated independence and socialism, quickly gaining popular support and becoming the main force of the independence movement.

events.title: Independence Movement Rises
events.description: Under Sékou Touré's leadership, the independence movement rose nationwide in Guinea. Worker strikes, student demonstrations and political rallies occurred frequently. French authorities attempted to suppress the movement, but nationalist sentiment continued rising.

events.title: Independence Referendum
events.description: In de Gaulle's French Community referendum, Guinea was the only French West African territory to vote against, with 95% of voters supporting immediate independence. This decision shocked France and the international community.

events.title: Guinea Independence
events.description: Guinea declared independence with Ahmed Sékou Touré as first president. France immediately withdrew all aid and technical personnel, even dismantling infrastructure. Guinea became the first independent nation in French West Africa.

events.title: Sékou Touré Dictatorship
events.description: Sékou Touré established a one-party socialist state with harsh dictatorial rule. Political opposition was suppressed, thousands imprisoned or executed. Failed economic policies led to poverty and isolation, but Touré maintained power for 26 years.

events.title: Portuguese Invasion Attempt
events.description: Portuguese forces launched an invasion from Guinea-Bissau attempting to overthrow Sékou Touré's government, as Guinea supported Guinea-Bissau's independence movement. The invasion failed but heightened regional tensions.

events.title: 'Women's Plot' Repression
events.description: Sékou Touré accused a group of women, including his ex-wife, of plotting a coup. Hundreds were arrested and executed in one of the bloodiest repressions of Touré's rule, demonstrating the regime's paranoia and brutality.

events.title: Sékou Touré's Death
events.description: Ahmed Sékou Touré died while receiving medical treatment in the United States, ending 26 years of dictatorial rule. His death opened a window of opportunity for political change in Guinea.

events.title: Lansana Conté Military Coup
events.description: Army Colonel Lansana Conté led a military coup, overthrowing Sékou Touré's successor and establishing military government. Conté promised economic reforms and eventual democratization.

events.title: Economic Liberalization Begins
events.description: Conté's government began implementing economic liberalization policies, abolishing the socialist economic system and introducing market mechanisms. The IMF and World Bank began providing aid to help economic reconstruction.

events.title: Multi-party Transition
events.description: Under international pressure, Conté's government began political liberalization. A new constitution was promulgated in 1991 allowing multi-party system. Opposition parties gained legal status, paving the way for democratic transition.

events.title: First Multi-party Elections
events.description: Guinea held its first multi-party presidential elections since independence. Lansana Conté won with 51.7% of votes, but the electoral process was controversial with opposition alleging fraud.

events.title: Military Rebellion Attempt
events.description: A group of officers attempted a coup to overthrow Conté's government, but the rebellion was quickly suppressed. This incident exposed military discontent and political instability.

events.title: Conté Re-elected
events.description: Lansana Conté won re-election in presidential elections with 56.1% of votes. Despite relatively peaceful elections, the opposition continued questioning electoral fairness.

events.title: Border Wars Begin
events.description: Rebels from Liberia and Sierra Leone began attacking Guinea's border regions. Hundreds of thousands of refugees flooded into Guinea, exacerbating humanitarian crisis. Government forces engaged in fierce battles with rebels.

events.title: Constitutional Amendment Controversy
events.description: Conté's government amended the constitution, removing presidential term limits and allowing him to seek a third term. This decision caused strong opposition and protests, viewed as democratic backsliding.

events.title: Conté's Third Election
events.description: Lansana Conté won a controversial third presidential term with 95.3% of votes. Major opposition parties boycotted the election, and international observers questioned its legitimacy.

events.title: National General Strike
events.description: Trade unions organized a national general strike protesting economic deterioration and government corruption. The strike lasted weeks, resulting in dozens of deaths. Conté was forced to appoint opposition leader Lansana Kouyaté as Prime Minister.

events.title: Conté's Death and Military Coup
events.description: Hours after Lansana Conté's death, Army Captain Moussa Dadis Camara led a military coup, dissolving government and parliament, establishing the 'National Council for Democracy and Development' military junta.

events.title: Stadium Massacre
events.description: The military junta suppressed an opposition rally at Conakry stadium, killing at least 157 people and sexually assaulting hundreds of women. This atrocity drew strong international condemnation and sanctions.

events.title: Camara Assassination Attempt
events.description: Military junta leader Moussa Dadis Camara was shot and wounded at the presidential palace, then sent to Morocco for treatment. Deputy Sékouba Konaté took power, promising democratic transition.

events.title: First Round Presidential Election
events.description: Guinea held the first round of presidential elections after democratic transition. Alpha Condé and Cellou Dalein Diallo advanced to the second round. The electoral process was relatively peaceful and gained international recognition.

events.title: Alpha Condé Elected President
events.description: Alpha Condé won the second round election with 52.5% of votes, becoming Guinea's first democratically elected president. The election marked the end of military rule and restoration of democratic institutions.

events.title: Military Barracks Attack
events.description: Armed men attacked the presidential residence and military barracks, killing several people. The government accused former junta members of plotting a coup attempt and arrested multiple suspects.

events.title: First Democratic Parliamentary Elections
events.description: Guinea held its first truly democratic parliamentary elections since independence. Despite some technical problems and delays, elections proceeded largely peacefully, marking an important step in democratic consolidation.

events.title: Ebola Epidemic
events.description: The West African Ebola epidemic broke out in Guinea, killing over 2,500 people. The epidemic severely impacted economic and social development, with international community providing extensive aid to help control the outbreak.

events.title: Alpha Condé Re-elected
events.description: Alpha Condé won re-election in presidential elections with 57.8% of votes. Despite opposition allegations of fraud, the election was generally considered free and fair.

events.title: Constitutional Amendment Protests
events.description: Alpha Condé proposed constitutional amendments that could allow him to seek a third term. This triggered massive protest movements with dozens killed in clashes. Opposition accused this of being authoritarian behavior.

events.title: New Constitution Referendum
events.description: Guinea held a new constitution referendum with 91.59% of voters supporting the new constitution. The new constitution reset presidential term limits, theoretically allowing Condé to run again. Opposition boycotted the referendum.

events.title: Condé's Third Election
events.description: Alpha Condé won a controversial third presidential term with 59.5% of votes. The election triggered violent clashes killing dozens. Opposition refused to recognize the results.

events.title: Mamady Doumbouya Military Coup
events.description: Special Forces Colonel Mamady Doumbouya led a military coup, arresting President Alpha Condé and dissolving government and parliament. Coup leaders established the 'National Committee for Reconciliation and Development,' promising political transition.

events.title: Doumbouya Sworn as Transitional President
events.description: Mamady Doumbouya was officially sworn in as transitional president, promising to hold elections within 36 months to restore civilian rule. International community condemned the coup, with ECOWAS imposing sanctions.

events.title: Transitional Government Governance
events.description: Doumbouya's transitional government began implementing reforms including fighting corruption, improving governance and preparing new elections. However, international sanctions continued and the economy faced challenges.

events.title: Political Transition Process
events.description: The transitional government continued advancing political transition, engaging in dialogue with opposition and civil society. New electoral and political party laws were drafted to prepare for future democratic elections.

events.title: Neolithic Culture
events.description: Archaeological discoveries show human activity in Guinea during the Neolithic period. Early inhabitants developed pottery making, stone tools and primitive agriculture. These early cultures laid the foundation for later Iron Age development.

events.title: Bantu Migration Influence
events.description: Although Bantu-speaking peoples mainly migrated southeast, their cultural and technological influence also reached Guinea. Agricultural techniques, iron-working and social organization improved, promoting population growth and social complexity.

events.title: Early Kingdom Formation
events.description: Small kingdoms and chiefdoms began forming across Guinea regions. These political entities controlled trade routes, iron mining and agricultural production. Social stratification was evident, with specialized craftsmen and merchant classes emerging.

events.title: Trans-Saharan Trade Participation
events.description: Northern Guinea regions began participating in trans-Saharan trade networks. Gold, ivory and slaves were exported northward in exchange for salt, horses and manufactured goods. This trade promoted economic development and cultural exchange.

events.title: Susu Kingdom Rise
events.description: The Susu people established a powerful kingdom in Guinea's coastal regions. They controlled important trading ports and inland trade routes, developing advanced agriculture and crafts. The Susu Kingdom became a major political force in the region.

events.title: Koniagui Kingdom Establishment
events.description: In present-day Conakry region, local tribes established the Koniagui Kingdom. This kingdom controlled important coastal trade and maintained trading relationships with the inland Mali Empire, serving as a crucial intermediary between coast and interior.

events.title: Fulani Southern Migration
events.description: Fulani pastoralists migrated south from the Sahel region into Guinea's highland areas. They brought advanced livestock techniques and Islamic faith, forming complex interactions with local agricultural societies.

events.title: Portuguese Trading Post Expansion
events.description: Portuguese established multiple trading posts along Guinea's coast, including in present-day Conakry and Boké regions. They signed trade agreements with local rulers and began systematic exploitation of the region's gold and ivory resources.

events.title: European Competition Intensifies
events.description: French, British and Dutch merchants began challenging Portuguese trade monopoly in Guinea. Various nations established competing trading posts along the coast, leading to complex local political situations and increased conflicts.

events.title: Slave Trade Institutionalization
events.description: Trans-Atlantic slave trade became institutionalized in Guinea. Local rulers and European merchants established complex slave supply networks, with inland warfare increasing to capture slaves, fundamentally changing social structures.

events.title: Futa Jallon Alliance Formation
events.description: Fulani Muslims in Guinea's central highlands formed political alliances, laying the foundation for later establishment of the Futa Jallon Islamic state. They began unifying scattered Fulani tribes and establishing common religious and political identity.

events.title: Futa Jallon Golden Age
events.description: The Futa Jallon Islamic state reached its peak, controlling vast territories from Senegal to Sierra Leone. The state established comprehensive administrative systems, military organization and educational institutions, becoming a major Islamic cultural center in West Africa.

events.title: British Abolition Act Impact
events.description: After Britain abolished the slave trade, it began patrolling West African coasts to combat slave ships. This had major economic impact on Guinea, forcing local rulers to seek new trade goods and economic models.

events.title: Legitimate Trade Transition
events.description: With the decline of slave trade, Guinea began transitioning to 'legitimate trade,' mainly exporting palm oil, groundnuts, ivory and gold. This transition changed production patterns and social relations but also brought new challenges.

events.title: French Military Conquest Begins
events.description: France began military conquest of Guinea's interior. French forces engaged in series of wars with local kingdoms, gradually expanding control. This marked colonial conquest expansion from coast to interior.

events.title: Futa Jallon Resistance Wars
events.description: The Futa Jallon Islamic state engaged in prolonged warfare with French colonial forces. Despite possessing modern weapons, Futa Jallon armies ultimately could not withstand sustained French offensives, gradually losing independence.

events.title: Conakry Establishment
events.description: France established the colonial city of Conakry on the mainland opposite Loos Islands, serving as French Guinea's administrative and commercial center. City planning followed European models, becoming a symbol of French colonial rule.

events.title: Berlin Conference Demarcation
events.description: The Berlin Conference determined European powers' spheres of influence in West Africa, with France gaining formal colonial rights over Guinea. This provided international legal basis for further French expansion in the region.

events.title: Colonial Administrative System Establishment
events.description: France established complete colonial administrative system in Guinea, including provincial, county and village three-tier management. Traditional rulers were incorporated into colonial system as indirect rule tools, but real power remained with French officials.

events.title: Forced Cultivation System
events.description: France implemented forced cultivation system in Guinea, requiring farmers to grow export crops like coffee, cocoa and cotton. This system disrupted traditional agriculture, leading to food shortages and social discontent.

events.title: World War I Impact
events.description: During World War I, thousands of Guineans were conscripted into French military service. The war increased colonial economic burden but also exposed some Guineans to the outside world, sparking national consciousness.

events.title: Great Depression Impact
events.description: The global Great Depression severely affected Guinea's economy, with export commodity prices plummeting and unemployment rising. France was forced to adjust colonial policies, but economic difficulties exacerbated social contradictions.

events.title: Vichy France Rule
events.description: During World War II, Guinea was under Vichy France rule. After 1940, it turned to Free France, providing strategic resources to the Allies. Wartime mobilization and sacrifice enhanced Guinean political awakening.

events.title: Post-war Political Awakening
events.description: After World War II, Guinea experienced political awakening waves. Veterans, intellectuals and workers began organizing political activities, demanding more rights and autonomy. This laid the foundation for later independence movements.

events.title: Labor Movement Rise
events.description: Guinean workers organized large-scale strikes under Sékou Touré's leadership, demanding improved working conditions and wages. The strikes gained widespread support, demonstrating organized labor movement power.

events.title: Educational Reform Movement
events.description: Guinean intellectuals promoted educational reform, demanding local language instruction and increased educational opportunities. This movement promoted national cultural consciousness awakening, providing ideological foundation for independence movement.

events.title: Loi-Cadre Implementation
events.description: France's Loi-Cadre gave Guinea greater internal autonomy, establishing local assemblies and government. Though limited, this reform provided practical experience for Guinean politicians.

events.title: Sékou Touré Elected Prime Minister
events.description: In local elections, Sékou Touré's Democratic Party of Guinea achieved overwhelming victory, with Touré elected as Guinea's Prime Minister. This marked decisive victory for independence faction in politics.

events.title: Post-Independence Economic Difficulties
events.description: In early independence period, Guinea faced severe economic difficulties. France's sudden withdrawal caused technical personnel shortage and infrastructure damage, with economy nearly collapsing. Government was forced to implement emergency measures to maintain basic operations.

events.title: Joining Non-Aligned Movement
events.description: Guinea became one of the founding members of the Non-Aligned Movement, establishing close relations with Yugoslavia, Egypt, India and other countries. This foreign policy helped Guinea maintain relative independence during the Cold War.

events.title: Currency Reform
events.description: Guinea withdrew from the franc zone and issued its own currency, the Guinean franc. This measure aimed to achieve economic independence but led to inflation and black market proliferation due to poor management.

events.title: 'Teachers' Plot' Case
events.description: Sékou Touré accused a group of teachers and intellectuals of plotting to overthrow the government, with hundreds arrested. This incident marked escalation of regime paranoia and beginning of systematic persecution of intellectuals.

events.title: 'Fulani Plot' Case
events.description: Government accused Fulani ethnic elites of plotting racial coup, conducting large-scale arrests of Fulani leaders. This repression exacerbated ethnic tensions and damaged national unity.

events.title: Women's Liberation Movement
events.description: Government promoted women's liberation movement, banning polygamy and promoting female education. Despite controversy, these measures somewhat improved women's status.

events.title: Market Liberalization Attempt
events.description: Facing economic crisis, government attempted limited market liberalization, allowing private small traders to operate. But these reforms were quickly reversed, and economy continued deteriorating.

events.title: Student Protest Movement
events.description: University students held protest activities demanding improved educational conditions and academic freedom. Government violently suppressed protests, closed universities and arrested student leaders.

events.title: Economic Crisis Intensifies
events.description: Guinea's economy fell into severe crisis with inflation exceeding 100% and basic commodity shortages. Government was forced to implement rationing system, but corruption and black markets worsened the situation.

events.title: Structural Adjustment Program
events.description: Conté government signed structural adjustment program with IMF, beginning large-scale economic reforms. Privatization, trade liberalization and fiscal austerity became main policy directions.

events.title: New Constitution Promulgated
events.description: Guinea promulgated new constitution formally establishing multi-party system and separation of powers. Constitution guaranteed basic human rights and political freedoms, providing legal framework for democratization process.

events.title: First Parliamentary Elections
events.description: Guinea held first multi-party parliamentary elections since independence. Despite some problems, elections proceeded largely peacefully with opposition parties gaining parliamentary seats.

events.title: Constitutional Crisis
events.description: During President Conté's serious illness, country fell into constitutional crisis. Military and civilian government disagreed over power succession, with political instability intensifying.

events.title: Strike Wave
events.description: Nationwide massive strike wave erupted protesting economic deterioration and government incompetence. Strikes lasted months, seriously affecting economic activities and social order.

events.title: Ethnic Conflicts
events.description: Ethnic conflicts erupted after presidential elections, mainly between Mandinka and Fulani peoples. Conflicts caused dozens of deaths, exposing deep ethnic tensions.

events.title: Local Elections
events.description: Guinea held first local elections since independence, electing mayors and local councilors. Elections strengthened local governance but also exposed electoral system imperfections.

events.title: Mining Reforms
events.description: Government promoted mining reforms, revising mining laws and requiring foreign companies to increase local investment and employment. Reforms aimed to let Guineans benefit more from mineral resource development.

events.title: Contemporary Challenges
events.description: Guinea faces multiple challenges: political transition uncertainty, economic difficulties, youth unemployment, inadequate infrastructure and governance issues. Despite rich mineral resources (world's largest bauxite reserves, iron ore, gold, diamonds), most of the population remains in poverty. International community continues pressuring for democratic restoration. Guinea's future depends on successfully completing political transition, achieving inclusive governance, and converting natural resource wealth into people's welfare.
